content: 1. The risk of selection bias due to random sequence generation and allocation concealment was unclear in the studies reviewed. This indicates that the methods used to randomly assign participants or conceal their allocation were not adequately described or assessed. 2. The risk of performance bias, which arises from the lack of blinding of participants and personnel, was also unclear. This suggests that the studies did not provide sufficient information on whether participants and researchers were blinded to the interventions being administered. 3. Detection bias, related to the blinding of outcome assessment, was similarly unclear. This means that it was not clear whether the individuals assessing the outcomes were aware of the participants' group assignments, which could influence the results. 4. Reporting bias, or selective reporting of outcomes, was judged to be of unclear risk. This implies that the studies may not have reported all pre-specified outcomes or selectively reported favorable results. 5. Other potential sources of bias, such as confounding factors, classification of exposures, departures from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), and selection of reported results, were also deemed to have unclear risks. This reflects a lack of transparency or detail in the study methodologies. 6. In the Blix 2017 study, data were collected from two large population-based pregnancy cohorts: the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC). Participants in MoBa were recruited between 1999 and 2008, while DNBC participants were recruited between 1996 and 2003. Information on infant feeding practices was obtained through mailed questionnaires and structured telephone interviews when the children were 6 and 18 months old. 7. The Brakohiapa 1988 study was a cross-sectional study involving 202 children aged 12 to 24 months who visited a hospital in Accra, Ghana. Mothers were interviewed about their children's weaning times and eating habits. The outcomes assessed included malnutrition, defined by specific weight-for-age, length-for-age, and weight-for-length thresholds. 8. The Burdette 2006 study followed 372 children prospectively from age 3 years, with body adiposity measured at age 5 years using DXA. Overweight and BMI were assessed, and inclusion criteria required children to be born after full-term gestation, free of chronic health problems, and with parents of the same race. 9. The Burke 2005 study involved participants from the Western Australian Pregnancy Cohort Study, with data collected on breastfeeding duration and repeated surveys conducted at 1, 3, 6, and 8 years of age. Breastfeeding categories were defined, and outcomes included adiposity, overweight, and BMI Z-scores. 10. The Butt 2014 study analyzed data from the Malmö Diet and Cancer Study, which included 17,035 women. Breastfeeding duration was assessed in relation to breast cancer subgroups, with exclusion criteria including prior breast cancer diagnosis, nulliparity, and insufficient data for analysis. 11. The Caleyachetty 2013 study followed a birth cohort in Mysore, India, to assess maternal risk factors and child health outcomes. Breastfeeding duration was categorized, and outcomes included high BMI and skinfold thickness at age 5 years. 12. The Camurdan 2011 study retrospectively analyzed growth data from infants born at Gazi University Hospital in Ankara, Turkey, and followed until age 4 years. Exclusive breastfeeding duration and total breastfeeding period were recorded, with BMI measured at various time points. 13. The Chaffee 2014 study followed a birth cohort in Porto Alegre, Brazil, to assess breastfeeding practices and dental health outcomes at 38 months. Breastfeeding duration and frequency were recorded, and dental status was evaluated using WHO protocols. 14. The Cheraghi 2013 study was a cross-sectional study of 385 children aged 3 to 6 years in Urmia, Iran. Data on breastfeeding practices were collected through questionnaires, and outcomes included underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity based on BMI percentiles. 15. The Chetwynd 2017 study analyzed data from the Black Women’s Health Study, a longitudinal cohort of 59,001 women. Hypertension was defined based on self-reported use of antihypertensive medications or physician-diagnosed hypertension. 16. The Choi 2017 study utilized data from the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) conducted between 2010 and 2013. This cross-sectional, nationally representative survey used multistage and stratified sampling methods.
